procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State appealed the Trial Court's acquittal to the High Court of Karnataka, Bench at Dharwad, in Criminal Appeal No. 100108 of 2014. The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused under Sections 148, 341, 504 and 326 read with 149 of IPC.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused, aggrieved by the High Court's conviction, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The conviction order passed by the High Court is set aside and the order of acquittal passed by the trial court is reaffirmed.
The appellants are to be released from custody forthwith.
Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court's order of acquittal.

facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, concluding that the prosecution had failed to prove the alleged offences beyond a reasonable doubt.
The State appealed this decision to the High Court.
The High Court reversed the trial court's order, convicted the accused, and sentenced them.
The accused then appealed the High Court's conviction to the Supreme Court.
law: A High Court should not interfere with a well-reasoned acquittal by a trial court unless there are strong and compelling reasons.
Interference is justified only where the trial court makes wrong assumptions of material facts or fails to appreciate the evidence properly.

If two reasonable views are possible from the evidence, the High Court should not reverse an acquittal merely because it would have taken the other view, as this indicates the prosecution has not proven guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court should not have re-appreciated the evidence in its entirety because there was no "grave infirmity" in the trial court's findings.
The Court noted that the prosecution's case suffered from several "contradictions and infirmities" which the trial court had rightly identified.
Specifically, there were material contradictions in witness statements regarding the assault and the participation of the accused.
The prosecution failed to prove the specific role and involvement of each accused person.
The Court also found the victims' actions to be "dubious," such as moving to a multi-specialty hospital without proper cause or documentation.
Given these weaknesses, the Court determined that the prosecution had failed to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no justification for the High Court to set aside the trial court's order of acquittal. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's conviction and reaffirmed the trial court's acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether a compromise between the parties can be a basis for quashing proceedings for non-compoundable offences.

facts: The parties involved in the case had entered into a compromise and executed a compromise deed.
The court was made aware of this compromise by the counsel for the appellants.
law: The court identified that the offences the accused were charged with were non-compoundable under Section 320 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The law does not permit giving legal effect to a compromise for non-compoundable offences.
application: The court explicitly stated that because the offences were non-compoundable, it could not give effect to the compromise.
Consequently, the court decided to disregard the compromise and adjudicate the appeal based on the merits of the case, such as the evidence on record and the findings of the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the compromise as a basis for quashing the proceedings. It explicitly stated that the compromise was not the basis for its conclusion and proceeded to acquit the accused on the merits of the case, finding that the prosecution had failed to prove their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial court correctly identified contradictions in the statements of prosecution witnesses P.W.1 and P.W.2.

facts: Prosecution witnesses P.W.1 and P.W.2 gave statements concerning an incident of assault and the participation of the accused.
The trial court found that the statements given by these two witnesses contained contradictions.
law: Contradictions in witness testimonies that are material to the case cannot be overlooked when assessing the evidence.
application: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's finding, stating that it had "rightly pointed out" the contradictions in the statements of P.W.1 and P.W.2.
The Court characterized these contradictions as "material ones" that specifically related to the details of the assault and the involvement of the accused persons.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the trial court was correct in identifying the material contradictions in the statements of prosecution witnesses P.W.1 and P.W.2, and that these contradictions could not be overlooked.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court's order of acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's order of conviction, argued that the High Court was not justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal.
respondent_arguments: The State argued in support of the High Court's judgment, contending that it was correct in convicting the appellants and overturning the trial court's acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a compromise between the parties can be a basis for quashing proceedings for non-compoundable offences.
appellant_arguments: The appellants noted that the parties had entered into a compromise, implicitly suggesting it as a factor for the court's consideration.
respondent_arguments: The State's position would be that for non-compoundable offences, a compromise is not a legal basis for quashing proceedings and the case must be decided on its merits.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the trial court correctly identified contradictions in the statements of prosecution witnesses P.W.1 and P.W.2.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that the trial court's decision to acquit was correct because it had rightly identified material contradictions in the statements of the prosecution witnesses.
respondent_arguments: The State, in defending the High Court's conviction, would have argued that the trial court erred in its assessment and that the contradictions were not significant enough to warrant an acquittal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court can only interfere in an appeal against acquittal if the trial court has made wrong assumptions of material facts or has failed to properly appreciate the evidence. If two reasonable views are possible based on the evidence, the High Court cannot reverse the acquittal, as this indicates the prosecution has not proven guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and the accused is entitled to the benefit of the doubt.
obiter: Even if the parties have entered into a compromise, the court must decide the matter on its merits when the alleged offences are not compoundable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution was not able to establish the guilt of the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt. The High Court should not have re-appreciated evidences in its entirety, especially when there existed no grave infirmity in the findings of the trial court. There exists no justification behind setting aside the order of acquittal passed by the trial court, especially when the prosecution case suffers from several contradictions and infirmities, and no specific assertion could be proved regarding the role and involvement of the accused persons.
legal_tests_applied: The High Court will interfere in appeals against acquittals, only where the trial court makes wrong assumptions of material facts or fails to appreciate the evidence properly.

If two views are reasonably possible from the evidence on record, one favouring the accused and one against the accused, the High Court is not expected to reverse the acquittal merely because it would have taken the view against the accused had it tried the case.
why_respondent_won: As the offences alleged are not compoundable, notwithstanding the fact that the parties have entered into a compromise, we will deal with the matter on merits.
policy_considerations: The very fact that two views are possible makes it clear that the prosecution has not proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and consequently the accused is entitled to benefit of doubt.
